Environmental Factors: Experiences such as childhood trauma or stress within the family may play a role in the development of OCD.

Upbringing and Personality Traits: Traits such as perfectionism and taking on excessive responsibility, as well as approaches to upbringing, may increase susceptibility to OCD.

Treatment for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT): CBT is one of the most effective treatments for OCD. It focuses on identifying and challenging obsessive thoughts and changing compulsive behaviours.

Medication: Antidepressants, particularly selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), can be effective in relieving OCD symptoms.

Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP): People are encouraged to face the triggers for their obsessions and refrain from carrying out their compulsions. This helps them better tolerate the obsessions and reduce compulsive behaviour.

Supportive Therapy and Counselling: Supportive therapy and counselling may also be offered to help people cope with difficulties in everyday life.

dissosiyatif-kimlik-bozuklug-u-nedir.title: What Is Dissociative Identity Disorder?
dissosiyatif-kimlik-bozuklug-u-nedir.excerpt: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a mental health condition in which a person displays two or more distinct identity states. The condition usually develops after…
parts:
Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a mental health condition in which a person displays two or more distinct identity states. It usually develops after severe trauma or abuse. DID is understood as an unconscious defence mechanism that helps a person distance themselves from traumatic experiences. Their different identity states, or alters, may have distinct personality traits, memories and ways of behaving.

What Are the Symptoms of Dissociative Identity Disorder?

The most prominent symptoms of DID are:

  • Identity Fragmentation: Experiencing two or more distinct identity states, also known as alters.
  • Memory Loss: Significant gaps in memory for personal history, important personal information and traumatic events.
  • Mental and Physical Difficulties: Depression, anxiety, impaired functioning and sometimes physical symptoms.
  • Changes in Perception: Changes in the way a person perceives reality and a sense of detachment from themselves.

Alters in People with Dissociative Identity Disorder

The alters seen in people with DID may be very different from their primary identity. Each alter may have a consistent identity, memories, behaviours and even distinct physical characteristics. Alters usually emerge to manage emotional stress or trauma the person cannot otherwise cope with and help them deal with these difficult experiences.

Which alter is in control may change in response to particular triggers, and the person may be unaware of these shifts. Switching between alters can have a serious effect on everyday life and the ability to function. Treatment for dissociative identity disorder is usually a long and challenging process in which psychotherapy and specialist support are essential.

What Causes Dissociative Identity Disorder (Multiple Personality Disorder)?

Severe Traumatic Events: DID usually develops after severe trauma in childhood. Physical, emotional and sexual abuse are among the most common traumatic experiences involved. Children may develop distinct identity states to make sense of and cope with such experiences. For example, a child experiencing physical abuse may develop another identity state to lessen the pain and fear. That identity state holds the painful memories and feelings, while the primary identity is shielded from those experiences.

Prolonged Neglect and Bullying: Childhood neglect and bullying can also contribute to the development of DID. Prolonged neglect or bullying within the family can leave a child without a safe, supportive environment. In such circumstances, a child may develop distinct identity states to protect themselves and cope with emotional wounds.

Trauma in Adolescence: Trauma in adolescence may also contribute to DID. Sexual abuse, severe bullying or other traumatic experiences at this age can have a profound psychological effect. Such events may lead young people to develop different defence mechanisms to protect themselves. Because adolescence is a crucial period for identity development, trauma at this age is thought to play an important role in the development of dissociative identity disorder.

How Common Is Dissociative Identity Disorder (Multiple Personality Disorder)?

DID is uncommon in the general population. Research suggests it affects about 1% of people. It is seen more often in women than in men, although this may be related to women reporting traumatic experiences more frequently.

Treatment for Dissociative Identity Disorder

Treatment for DID is a long-term, multifaceted process tailored to each person’s needs. Its main elements are:

Long-Term Psychotherapy: In-depth psychotherapy helps people face their traumatic past and work towards integration between different identity states. It focuses on processing trauma, understanding the different identity states and helping them work together.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT): CBT techniques can help people with DID change patterns of thought and behaviour. This therapy helps them identify negative thought patterns and replace them with healthier ones.

Medication: Medication may be used to relieve depression, anxiety and other emotional or mental health difficulties associated with DID. Antidepressants and anti-anxiety medicines may improve a person’s overall emotional wellbeing.

Supportive Therapy: Supportive techniques can improve daily life and help people maintain social functioning and relationships. This approach helps them cope with everyday challenges and improve their social relationships.

The success of DID treatment depends largely on the person’s engagement with the process and their motivation. Treatment is often difficult and emotionally intense, but the right support and methods can significantly improve quality of life.

psikolojik-uyusma-ve-karincalanma-nasil-.title: How Can You Ease Stress-Related Numbness and Tingling?
psikolojik-uyusma-ve-karincalanma-nasil-.excerpt: Stress-related numbness and tingling are physical sensations often associated with psychological states such as stress or anxiety. In this article…
parts:
Stress-related numbness and tingling are physical sensations often associated with psychological states such as stress or anxiety. In this article, we’ll look at how to recognise these sensations, what causes them and how to cope with them.

How Can You Recognise Stress-Related Tingling and Numbness?

Stress-related tingling and numbness are temporary changes in sensation that can occur in different parts of the body, especially the hands, feet or face. They can feel like pins and needles, burning or coldness. These sensations usually appear during moments of anxiety or stress and draw your attention to what you are feeling in your body.

What Causes Stress-Related Numbness and Tingling?

Stress-related numbness and tingling are often associated with stress, anxiety, panic attacks or intense emotions. These states heighten the body’s alertness and trigger physiological responses. As a result, the nervous system can become overstimulated, leading to sensations such as numbness or tingling.

Under stress or anxiety, the body goes into ‘fight or flight’ mode. This increases the release of adrenaline, which can affect blood flow and the nervous system. Changes in breathing under stress, such as breathing quickly or shallowly, can also affect oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body and cause numbness or tingling. These reactions are usually temporary and tend to ease or disappear when the underlying stress or anxiety is managed.

How Long Do Stress-Related Numbness and Tingling Last?

How long stress-related numbness and tingling last varies from person to person and depends on what triggered them. They usually pass when the underlying cause, such as stress or anxiety, subsides. Sometimes they ease within a few minutes, but they can last longer. Persistent or recurring numbness and tingling can be a sign of a more serious health problem and may need medical assessment.

For example, numbness and tingling during a panic attack may subside quickly once the attack passes. If the sensations persist or keep recurring over a period of time, however, a more thorough assessment may be needed. For people under constant stress, these sensations can last longer and feel more intense. If they affect daily life or cause significant discomfort, it is important to speak to a healthcare professional.

How Can You Ease Stress-Related Numbness and Tingling?

The following approaches can help ease stress-related numbness and tingling:

  1. Relaxation Techniques: Deep breathing, meditation and yoga can help relax your body and calm your mind. These techniques can ease physical tension caused by anxiety or stress.
  2. Physical Activity: Regular exercise can improve your mood and lower stress by increasing the release of endorphins. Walking, running, cycling or swimming can improve circulation and may help ease numbness and tingling.
  3. Enough Sleep and Rest: Good-quality sleep is essential for the body to repair itself and regain balance. Improving your sleep routine and getting enough rest may help with stress-related numbness and tingling.
  4. A Balanced Diet: A healthy, balanced diet helps the body cope with stress. Eating foods rich in vitamins and minerals can support the health of your nervous system.
  5. Professional Help and Counselling: If these symptoms persist or affect your everyday life, it is important to consult a healthcare professional. Psychotherapy or counselling can help you manage stress and improve your emotional health.

If you are experiencing symptoms of an anxiety disorder, such as stress-related numbness or tingling, and are unsure what is causing them, you can contact us for support.

love-bombing-nedir-sevgi-bombardimani-bi.title: What Is Love Bombing? | Is Love Bombing a Form of Manipulation?
love-bombing-nedir-sevgi-bombardimani-bi.excerpt: What Is Love Bombing? Love bombing is a pattern of behaviour in which someone showers their partner with affection, attention, praise and gifts at the start of a relationship…
parts:
What Is Love Bombing?

Love bombing is a pattern of behaviour in which someone showers their partner with affection, attention, praise and gifts at the start of a relationship. It is often intended to create emotional attachment and dependence and can turn into manipulation over time.

Love bombing happens when one person shows the other intense affection, attention and tenderness at the start of a romantic relationship. It often takes the form of exaggerated praise, constant contact, intense emotional attachment and a flood of gifts. Because it involves an imbalance of power and a disregard for personal boundaries, it is generally seen as a manipulative strategy. It can be used to create dependence and gain control.

How Can You Tell If You Are Being Love Bombed?

Signs that you may be experiencing love bombing include:

  1. Excessive attention and romantic gestures early in the relationship.
  2. Your partner constantly sends messages full of praise.
  3. The relationship moves much faster than usual.
  4. Your partner idealises you to an extreme degree.
  5. Strong demands for commitment and a serious relationship early on.

If your partner showers you with praise, constantly buys you gifts and gives you an overwhelming amount of attention early in the relationship, it may be a sign of love bombing. These displays of affection are often too intense to sustain.

Why Can Giving or Receiving Too Much Affection Be Harmful?

Giving or receiving excessive affection can create unhealthy attachment and dependence in a relationship. Such relationships are often unbalanced and can lead to one person emotionally manipulating the other.

Genuine emotional needs and healthy relationship boundaries can also be ignored. Over time, this can undermine personal freedom and self-esteem and may even cause emotional harm. It can leave the partner emotionally dependent and easier to control.

What Are the Stages of Love Bombing?

  1. Intense Attention and Romance: Excessive attention, romantic gestures and displays of admiration at the start of the relationship.
  2. Rapid Progress and Pressure to Commit: The relationship moves faster than usual, with early declarations of love and strong demands for commitment.
  3. Growing Emotional Attachment and Dependence: The person being targeted becomes emotionally dependent and more likely to go along with what the manipulator wants.
  4. Control and Manipulation: The balance of power in the relationship shifts, and the manipulator begins to use tactics to control and manipulate the other person.

What Does Love Bombing Look Like? 10 Signs

  1. Exaggerated displays of affection and attention early in the relationship.
  2. A flood of gifts and over-the-top gestures.
  3. Constant praise and idealisation.
  4. Excessive jealousy and possessiveness.
  5. A relationship that moves unusually fast.
  6. Emotional manipulation and attempts to make you feel guilty.
  7. Attempts by your partner to dominate your life.
  8. Excessive demands for commitment and seriousness.
  9. Violations of personal boundaries.
  10. An imbalance of power in the relationship.

What Can You Do If It Happens to You?

  1. Recognise Your Feelings: Notice what you feel in the relationship and what makes you uncomfortable.
  2. Set and Maintain Your Boundaries: Establish healthy personal boundaries and uphold them.
  3. Get an Outside Perspective: Ask trusted friends or a therapist how they see the situation.
  4. Slow Down the Relationship: Take things more slowly and think carefully about each step.
  5. Seek Professional Help: Consider getting professional support to understand the situation and make healthy decisions.

If you are experiencing love bombing, it is important to set and maintain personal boundaries. Be cautious when a relationship moves very quickly and try to let it develop at a natural pace. If you sense manipulation, it may help to discuss it with a professional and get an outside perspective. Make decisions with your own emotional needs and expectations for a healthy relationship in mind.

A Few Tips from a Relationship Therapist

  1. Understand Your Emotional Attachment: Try to get clear about your emotional needs and expectations.
  2. Set Realistic Expectations: Decide what you can realistically expect from the relationship and stick to those expectations.
  1. Communicate Openly: Share your feelings and concerns openly with your partner.
  2. Give Yourself Time: Take time to assess the relationship and avoid rushing.
  3. Maintain Your Independence: Keep your independence and make time for your hobbies while building a healthy relationship.

These suggestions can help you build a healthy, balanced relationship and protect yourself from the effects of manipulative behaviour such as love bombing.

If you would like more information or support, you can contact me on Instagram:

https://www.instagram.com/aynurtumen/

You can find my contact details on my Instagram profile.

askin-bilimsel-tanimi-nedir.title: What Is the Scientific Definition of Love?
askin-bilimsel-tanimi-nedir.excerpt: ‘I’m past all that! Who falls in love at my age?’ Do you ever say that? Have you lost all faith in love? Maybe you feel you can’t live with it or without it. Perhaps…
parts:
‘I’m past all that! Who falls in love at my age?’ Do you ever say that? Have you lost all faith in love? Maybe you feel you can’t live with it or without it. Perhaps you’re looking for an explanation and an answer when it comes to love…

Scientists have long worked out what happens in the body when we fall in love. The scientific explanation is that we release large amounts of adrenaline and serotonin and a little oxytocin. We owe the excitement, motivation and happiness we feel when we’re in love to those chemicals.

Isn’t it strange that brain chemicals and hormones can offer a scientific explanation for the romance we experience? The chemicals in our brains have been shown to stir feelings of love. The same brain region that awakens love also gives rise to maternal instincts and romantic feelings.

We also know that these instincts ultimately exist to enable reproduction and ensure the survival of the species. In other words, love emerged as a way to keep women and men together so the species would survive.

In many studies, researchers have run experiments to distinguish love from other kinds of relationships and emotional states. When participants were shown a range of photographs, their reactions settled. But when they saw a photograph of the person they loved, researchers observed an unusually large increase in all the chemicals, hormones and secretions mentioned above.

When people who said they were in love were asked how they felt, many reported similar symptoms. Usually there is a feeling of inexplicable joy and excitement, along with a strange, equally inexplicable nervousness and a heart that races like mad. According to researchers, these seemingly inexplicable feelings are caused by the brain releasing phenylethylamine, a natural amphetamine. The adrenal glands then pump adrenaline and noradrenaline into the body. These hormones are known for helping the body cope with stress.

Love, however, produces a positive kind of stress. You know how people say they felt butterflies in their stomach when they fell in love? Those very hormones are what give rise to that physical sensation.

Suddenly, love claims its place at the centre of our lives. The person you’re in love with becomes the focus of your passion. When you can’t think of anyone else, you may sometimes wonder whether you’re losing your mind.

Research also suggests that a 40% drop in serotonin, the chemical in the brain linked to obsessive-compulsive disorder, has the same effect when you fall in love. A 40% drop in serotonin is observed during that period. The drop in serotonin can give rise to anxiety and depression.

In such cases, people experience love as painful rather than joyful. But this is temporary… When researchers repeated the measurements after a year with the person they loved, serotonin levels were found to have returned to normal…

askla-ilgili-inanclarimizin-olusma-esigi.title: When Our Beliefs About Love Take Shape
askla-ilgili-inanclarimizin-olusma-esigi.excerpt: We record everything we encounter through sounds, sights, smells and, in short, all five senses. Throughout this book, I’ll call the label that is imprinted on our subconscious a code…
parts:
We record everything we encounter through sounds, sights, smells and, in short, all five senses. Throughout this book, I’ll call the label that is imprinted on our subconscious a code. The codes we store, ready to be recalled when needed, shape our lives without our consciously choosing it.

We create the life we imagine. We give things meaning through our thoughts, what we take from our experiences and everything that has influenced us since childhood. These definitions guide everything in our lives. In other words, the love we experience matches the way we have coded love. That is because we also build our lives around those codes.

Our codes therefore guide us in our love lives, and we use them as building blocks for our lives. When one of these stored codes is called up, it is matched to the scene we are experiencing. Coding happens at moments when we decide, ‘This is what this means.’ In making that association, we give the experience a label.

For example, we might label something ‘a happy moment’, ‘an unhappy, bad moment’, ‘danger’ or ‘nothing to be afraid of’.

Codes are labels that can be called up again… The important point is that these associations form without our consciously choosing them. Once we become aware of them, they are easier to change. Here’s how it works. Because these associations have been anchored thousands of times in the past, when we encounter something new, the subconscious easily matches it to a scene it coded before. These labels sometimes make life easier and sometimes make it harder. The scenes we associate with fear are labelled in our subconscious between birth and the age of seven.

Something coded as frightening keeps bringing up fear for that person. Let me illustrate how these associations and recalls work with an example in one of my clients’ own words:

‘When I was a child, I was hit by a red car. There was a smell of burning at the time, although it might have been meat cooking at the snack bar on the corner. Years later, I was invited to a picnic. My boyfriend came to pick me up in a red car. I started feeling tense. He drove so fast all the way to the picnic spot that I became even more tense. That day, the smell of burnt meat on the barbecue and the red car filled me with a sense of unease and anxiety that I couldn’t explain. I was unhappy and unsettled, and I couldn’t work out why. The person I loved was beside me, but I was in a panic. That was the day my relationship ended. Everything fell apart. Now I understand a little of why it happened.’

My client’s painful experience had left its mark on her. The accident had become associated with the colour red. The red car and the smell of burnt meat had formed a negative code for her.

When she unexpectedly encountered that combination again, the colour red and a smell of burning, it brought back the earlier scene. Without realising it, she recreated that scene and felt a tension she could not explain. In our conversations, she came to see that even years later, the accident was behind her dislike of red, her aversion to red cars and her inability to eat meat. People do not always know what lies behind some of their behaviours.

Once a scene like that comes back to mind, it is possible to change the code. A new, positive memory can be formed around the colour red, which she has come to dislike.

aynur-tumen-ile-aile-dizimi-alan-terapi-.title: What Are Family Constellation, Field Therapy and Constellation Work with Aynur Tümen?
aynur-tumen-ile-aile-dizimi-alan-terapi-.excerpt: This is a practical, phenomenological form of bodywork. It draws its strength from ‘REPRESENTATIVE PERCEPTION’. ‘Perceptions we have absorbed without noticing, things we don’t know we know, emerge through the work…
parts:
This is a practical, phenomenological form of bodywork. It draws its strength from ‘REPRESENTATIVE PERCEPTION’.

‘Perceptions we have absorbed without noticing, things we don’t know we know, emerge through the work.

The work helps people recognise old perceptions, beliefs, patterns and judgements stored within them through a deeper, bodily form of knowing beyond conscious thought and logic. They can then reorder their place in their own system and make room for new perceptions.

When this happens, people feel lighter and full of joy. They gradually see recurring problems begin to come to an end and see things from a different perspective. Life stops being a source of suffering and becomes a source of happiness in all its richness.

We are each one member of an enormous system that includes those who came before us, whether they are still alive or have died, and those who will come after us.

Our place in this wider system is determined by the ‘perceptions’ that develop from birth through the family we are born into and grow up in, especially through our attachment to our mother and later through our bond with our father and immediate family.

If these perceptions have developed in a way that allows us to move forward from the place we actually occupy in our family system, and we are not unconsciously caught up in other people’s trauma within that system, we can go through life with ease, joy and success. We can be resilient, willing to find common ground and healthy in body, mind and spirit.

A family system may contain losses, early deaths, divorces, betrayals of all kinds, migration, murder, abuse, the exclusion of people or events generally deemed ‘unacceptable’, and similar traumas. If a person unknowingly takes these on through attachment, out of ‘blind love’ and a need to belong, it disrupts their place in the system and the natural course of their life. This can show up as recurring problems, addictions or dependencies they recognise but cannot overcome, outbursts of anger, relationship difficulties in their personal or professional life, unexplained deep unhappiness, shame, resentment, irritability, sleeplessness, confusion, money problems, repeated behaviours driven by deep fear and anxiety, postural problems or chronic health problems.

Early in life, before a person’s thinking has developed, information conveyed through attachment to the mother is registered through emotions in the body and its cells.

A newborn knows they are in their mother’s arms with their whole body and every cell, without having to think. In the same way, they sense that their mother loves them, cares about them, notices them and protects them. Just as they ‘know’ these things, they also absorb, like a sponge, information about any anxiety, insecurity, fear or trauma their mother carries, through their attachment to her.

The phenomenological approach and bodily experiences used in this work can help people access this information and revise what was recorded at the time the problem arose.

HOW ARE AYNUR TÜMEN’S SESSIONS CONDUCTED?

Aynur Tümen offers sessions on trauma and intention, family, love, success, sexuality, abuse, harassment, success and health, as well as organisational work.

Sessions can generally take place in a group or individually. In group sessions, people other than the client take part as ‘representatives’ of individuals or events connected to the issue the client brings.

The main difference from psychodrama is that the representatives do not need to know what the client’s issue is.

Group sessions involve a facilitator, representatives and the client.

Individual sessions involve a facilitator and the client, with symbolic objects used in the work.
